title: How does one start?
author: PANC0NE
selftext:
Greetings!

I am curious about the process, from the first step to the finish line, what do i need to start? Beside an idea

replies.author: syn_krown
replies.body: In all seriousness, all you need is a claude pro subscription and a clear idea of your game(for me, I get it to build an editor so I can still make the game), ask it to use html and javascript and any libraries for optimal performance, and Opus 5.5 will do it. Might take some testing to find where it falls short then upload back to claude with the changes you wanna have done. The claude website is enough to do it.

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: HTML+CSS+JS can go a long way if you just want to see your ideas take form. As your AI to build  you a web page with the game idea you have. Then iterate.

comments.author: affabledrunk
comments.body: You ask the model itself whats best to match your idea. And even if you go wrong (i.e. you choose to not use a game engine and later on you figure out you need one), its so trivial to have the model rework it for you. As you seem a total clueless noob, i recommened you do some three.js crap browser game first to explore your ideas quickly, if you need all the bells and whistles and you want to actually release a game, you can have the model rework it for you then. Good luck!

replies.author: PANC0NE
replies.body: thank you! i'll look into it

comments.author: Blake9712
comments.body: If you’re starting from scratch with nothing I’d start with a sort of throwaway idea and make it as good as you possibly can, then when you figure out the fun value of your idea, the mistakes, then I’d start with what you really want. But to answer directly, you can literally go to Claude code and ask it to make you a game. It is better if you set up a git repo and all that but you can ask Claude how to do that.

comments.author: DudeWithASweater
comments.body: Have an idea, pick an AI model, pick a coding language, go to work.

comments.author: EffectNo2152
comments.body:
I built a setup where I can control most of my game-development workflow from my phone, while my Windows PC does the actual heavy work.  
The basic idea is:  
**Phone = control panel**  
**AI = planner/operator**  
**PC = development machine**  
**Blender = 3D asset factory**  
**Vite = live testing**  
**GitHub = source control + automation**  
**itch.io = deployment**  
The main tools:  
**ChatGPT / coding model** — I describe what I want in normal language. It plans changes, writes code, debugs, and coordinates the other tools.  
**ECC / Hermes Agent** — agent harnesses/orchestration tools. They help give the AI a structured workflow instead of just randomly writing code.  
**Desktop Commander / Remote Desktop Commander** — lets the AI access my Windows PC’s terminal and files so it can actually run commands, edit projects, launch servers, use Git, run Blender jobs, etc.  
**Windows PC** — this is where the real work happens. It runs Blender, Node, Python, Git, game projects, build tools, and local services.  
**Vite** — runs the game locally in a browser.  
**Hot Module Reload (HMR)** — when the AI changes code, Vite updates the running game almost instantly so I can test changes fast.  
**LAN / Tailscale** — lets my phone connect to the development PC. On my home network I can open the local Vite build directly on my phone. Tailscale can make this work remotely in a safer way.  
**Blender** — creates the 3D assets.  
**Blender Python** — lets the AI generate or modify models, materials, scenes, lighting, exports, and validation automatically with scripts.  
**Blender MCP** — another way to expose Blender tools directly to AI agents.  
**MCP (Model Context Protocol)** — a standard way for AI models to call tools instead of only chatting.  
**Asset Forge** — my own pipeline built around Blender automation. It takes a request, plans the asset, generates it, adds materials/details, validates it, exports it, and saves useful parts for reuse.  
**Asset/material library** — successful materials, models, foliage, decals, geometry pieces, etc. are saved so future jobs can reuse them instead of rebuilding everything.  
**OpenStreetMap** — provides things like roads, buildings, and map layout data.  
**USGS/public terrain data** — provides real elevation and terrain data for building real-world maps.  
**Three.js / Godot** — game engines/runtime tools I use for different projects.  
**Python** — automation glue for Blender, processing, tools, and pipelines.  
**Node.js / npm** — runs Vite, web tooling, JavaScript game projects, and local servers.  
**ElevenLabs** — generates voices, announcers, radio characters, dialogue, and audio.  
**Kokoro / local TTS** — local speech generation for large amounts of dialogue without relying completely on paid APIs.  
**Suno** — music generation experiments for things like in-game radio.  
**Git** — tracks changes and lets me undo bad AI edits.  
**GitHub** — stores the projects, branches, history, and automation.  
**GitHub Actions** — automatically runs builds/tests/deployment jobs.  
**Butler** — itch.io’s command-line upload tool.  
**itch.io** — hosts playable builds.  
The workflow looks like this:  
**I type a request on my phone**  
↓  
**AI plans the work**  
↓  
**AI connects to the development PC**  
↓  
**Edits code / runs Blender / generates assets or audio**  
↓  
**Vite updates the game**  
↓  
**I test it live on my phone**  
↓  
**I say what looks broken**  
↓  
**AI fixes it and tests again**  
↓  
**Git saves the working version**  
↓  
**GitHub stores it**  
↓  
**GitHub Actions builds it**  
↓  
**Butler deploys it to itch.io**  
The main idea is that the AI is not magically making an entire game from one prompt.  
The useful part is giving the AI access to real tools and a feedback loop:  
**plan → build → test → see what broke → fix → test again → save → deploy**  
If you wanted to copy this setup as a beginner, start simple:  
Install Git, Node.js, Python, Blender, and Vite.  
Put your project in GitHub.  
Set up remote access to your development PC.  
Run the project with Vite so you can test changes instantly.  
Learn basic Blender Python for asset automation.  
Add AI tools like ChatGPT, ElevenLabs, or local TTS.  
Add GitHub Actions later for automated builds/deployments.  
Keep every experimental change in Git so you can undo mistakes.  
You do **not** need every part on day one.  
The simplest useful version is:  
**AI + remote PC access + Git + Vite + Blender**  
Everything else can be added later.

comments.author: deReaLizedGames
comments.body:
The more you flesh out the idea in your head and get as detailed as possible with how you want the mechanics to work the better the output you'll get. 

At the same time, be flexible with how you implement your ideas. AI has a lot of limitations; you will make a much better game if you lean into those limits rather than try to fight against them. For example, it's not good at fully realistic graphics, but it can pull of stylized graphics really well, so go with that. It can't do animations well, so design game mechanics or pick characters that still look good with suboptimal animations. Procedural animation works way better than authored animations so I'd go that route. 

If you want to make a 3D game, I recommend three.js and have Claude make all assets in Blender (super easy, you just have to have Blender installed and it'll do everything, you don't even need to open it). That workflow will be so much easier for your first game and still produce good results, especially if your graphics are stylized.

Start with a small vertical slice - the base mechanics, a small level. Refine the mechanics first so they feel good, then start building on top of that solid groundwork. 

Making a prototype with AI is the easy part, the part that really takes time and effort is making that prototype good. The most important part though is to just enjoy it! If you enjoy the process itself you'll be motivated to keep going, rather than give up after a few weeks. A ***good*** game will take months, even with AI. But also, if it's just a hobby for fun, you don't have to make a "good" game. If you have fun making 20 prototypes that's perfectly fine too. Just know what you want to get out of it going in.

Good luck!!

comments.author: fluxtah
comments.body: Start with the smallest thing that works, make well defined architectural boundaries as project matures, add useful harness tools to keep agent in the loop. Test the hell out of it, manage your workload as issues on gh both bugs and features (ephemeral details). Have a shared language with your agent (project glossary) keep long lived docs in your repo (architectural decisions, feature specs, etc).

comments.author: dgeisert
comments.body:
The best way to start is to start.  Join us in an AI based game jam and just make something.  Do it quickly and learn, then do it again.

[https://itch.io/jam/jamference-ai-game-jam-hack-1](https://itch.io/jam/jamference-ai-game-jam-hack-1)

comments.author: Valdaraak
comments.body:
You talk to Claude and experiment. Learn the capabilities, learn the limitations.

Basically, you start by doing.

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body:
Build, play, repeat. Just do this every day for the next month and you’ll be astounded how far you can go. Once you have a game concept get codex or Claude to build the first working version in a one shot, test it, figure out what’s good and bad, tell the AI, and on and on. You’ll figure it out as you go if you put in the work. 

Don’t be afraid to throw things away. I threw away nearly 10 games in a couple weeks before I found one that’s worth working on long term. Build fast, test early, shitcan the bad ones and keep learning.
